title: Canary traffic shard heuristics and state-rewind run notes
content:
Purpose:
This is a working note describing a probe-driven, shard-based canary pattern for private (VPC/on-prem) Redwood deployments. It focuses on how we pick traffic shards, when and how we trigger state-rewind (for KV/cached state), and a fast bisect/rollback method for identifying problematic runtime/control-plane changes during upgrades.

Motivation / problem statement:
- Private environments have heterogeneous hardware and variable network topologies; a 10% canary may behave fine in one cluster but fail in another.
- Stateful components (in-memory caches, local KV, ephemeral shard-local checkpoints) make rolling upgrades riskier because traffic split + state skew can cause inconsistent behavior.
- We need a repeatable, low-footprint way to surface regressions quickly and unwind state changes safely.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to private deployments using the Redwood control plane (private control plane) with a per-customer routing shim.
- Assumes deployment is backed by HA storage for persistent state and an eventually-consistent cache layer that can be invalidated.
- Terraform is used to provision routing and feature-flag gates (we include notes below).

High-level approach:
1) Create multiple shards keyed by low-cardinality attributes (region, rack group, capacity class). Start with 3 logical shards: probe shard (0.5% traffic), small canary shards (2x 5%), broad canary (20%).
2) Use active probes (synthetic requests) injected into each shard to validate basic correctness, latency, and error signatures before escalating traffic.
3) For stateful nodes, run a staged state-rewind capability that can roll back in-memory deltas without touching persistent storage. Only when in-memory rewind is not possible do we fallback to restoring from persistent snapshots.
4) If probes detect regressions, run a bisect across candidate artifacts (runtime, model binary, kernel/driver change, config flags) using a traffic binary search across shards.

Shard selection heuristics (practical rules):
- Prefer to put probe shard on the least-loaded, most-isolated node group (to avoid noisy neighbors).
- Canary shards should be mapped to nodes that mirror production characteristics: one shard on GPU-majority nodes, one on CPU-only nodes.
- If hardware heterogeneity > 15% (by compute class), create an extra canary shard to represent the minority class.
- Avoid placing canaries on nodes currently in maintenance or recently drained.
- Always tag shards with telemetry labels (hw_class, tf_version, driver_hash).

Probe design and metrics to watch (synthetic probes):
- Synthetic probes must be representative of top-10 production paths. Use recorded traces with stable inputs. Keep probe QPS low (0.1–1/sec per shard) but frequent (every 5–15s).
- Key metrics: 95p latency, error rate (4xx/5xx split), model output divergence score (when applicable), and token-level anomaly counts.
- Profiler probes: short sequences to exercise large attention windows and kv-cache hot paths.
- Compare probe outputs vs golden baseline using fuzzy similarity; mark a probe fail if similarity < threshold or latency > threshold.

State-rewind model (conceptual):
- Goal: let canary traffic mutate ephemeral state locally and then safely rewind those changes if the canary is aborted, without needing full DB restore.
- Components:
  - Local mutation log: each node keeps a small, append-only delta log for ephemeral state mutations with timestamps and causal IDs.
  - Rewind policy: if canary aborted within X minutes (configurable), nodes apply reverse mutations from the local log in reverse causal order.
  - Safe flush: nodes write a tombstone marker to persistent logs when a rewind occurs to prevent future replay.
- Limitations: full rewind is not guaranteed if the node evicted or crashed; in that case, we fallback to persistent snapshot-based restore.

Runbook (step-by-step upgrade procedure using shards):
1) PREP: create canary artifacts and mark in TF: set feature flag canary_enabled = true for shard ids. Export snapshots from persistent store (last good).
2) PROVISION: allocate shards via Terraform routing module (see TF notes below). Assign probe shard to isolated group.
3) DRY-RUN: deploy artifact to probe shard only. Start synthetic probes and wait for 10–15 minutes of green.
4) SMALL-CANARIES: if probe green, roll to both 5% canaries concurrently (different hw classes). Run probes and production light traffic for 30–60 minutes.
5) BROAD-CANARY: expand to 20% if prior green. Continue probing and run heavier load benchmarks.
6) GRADUAL-PROMOTE: escalate in increments (20→40→100) with health windows (30–60m) and canary gating.
7) ABORT / REWIND: if probes fail at any stage:
   - Immediately mark canary shards read-only for writes to persistent layer (if possible).
   - Trigger local state-rewind on affected nodes. Command: curl -X POST https://private-control-plane/_internal/rewind?shard=<id>
   - If local rewind fails or nodes missing, schedule snapshot restore and redirect traffic away from corrupted nodes.
8) POST-MORTEM: capture probe results, diffs, and node logs. Start bisect as needed.

Terraform notes (practical snippets and invariants):
- Keep routing shards as HCL-managed short-lived resources, not long-lived objects. Example minimal module usage: 

module \"canary-routing\" {
  source = \"git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/infrastructure.git//modules/canary-routing\"
  shards = [\"probe-1\", \"canary-a\", \"canary-b\", \"broad-canary\"]
  weights = {\"probe-1\" = 0.005, \"canary-a\" = 0.05, \"canary-b\" = 0.05, \"broad-canary\" = 0.2}
  labels = {env = var.env, team = \"runtime\"}
}

- Invariants to enforce in TF plan: do not change shard topology and assignments in the same apply that changes runtime binaries. Separate into two applies (routing apply then artifact apply).
- Add a terraform-preflight plan check that validates probes are scheduled and metrics hooks exist. Fail early if probe hooks are missing.

Fast bisect procedure (finding bad artifact/config):
- When a canary fails, we often have multiple candidate causes. Use a binary-split traffic recomposition:
  1) identify N candidate artifacts (e.g., runtime v1, model v2, driver patch).
  2) run a short (5–10 minute) experiment toggling half the failing shard traffic to artifact A and half to artifact B while keeping probe traffic unchanged.
  3) Observe divergence; if artifact A passes, promote it to remaining shard; otherwise narrow search.
- Automation tip: have a playbook-script able to reassign weights and revert within 60s.

Safety checks and hard abort triggers:
- Immediate global abort if: 5xx rate increases by > 300% absolute or p95 latency doubles vs baseline across any probe shard.
- Abort and isolate if model output similarity drops below 0.6 on any probe path for two consecutive windows.
- If disk corruption or eviction seen on any canary node, start snapshot restore for that node and exclude it from routing until restored.

Observability and telemetry requirements:
- Must tag every canary request with shard_id, artifact_hash, and cohort_id.
- Probes must log full payload and model outputs (obfuscated PII) to a retained bucket for 72 hours for debug.
- Dashboard: canary-overview showing shard-level errors, rewind events, and bisect state.

Post-upgrade checklist (if successful):
- Verify rewind logs are empty (no pending rewinds).
- Remove probe records and reduce synthetic probe frequency after 72 hours if stable.
- Collapse shards back to default routing topology via a controlled TF apply.

Open questions / TODOs (action items):
- Define exact rewind time-window default (currently propose 30 minutes).
- Add CLI support to force a check-only rewind dry-run against a node.
- Improve local mutation log compaction: currently naive, will grow if canary runs are long.
- Add TF preflight plugin that queries the private control plane to assert probe wiring.

Appendix: quick commands and helpers
- Reassign weight (internal): curl -X PATCH https://private-control-plane/api/route -d '{\"shard\":\"canary-a\",\"weight\":0.0}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'
- Trigger rewind (internal): curl -X POST https://private-control-plane/_internal/rewind?shard=canary-a
- TF dry-run pattern: terraform plan -var-file=canary-vars.tfvars -out canary.plan && terraform apply canary.plan

Notes about provenance: this doc is a sketch capturing a hybrid of the runtime team's observed failures from Q4 2024 and current TF routing constraints. It's intentionally conservative about state rewinds because some tenants use encrypted on-disk caches that must not be tampered with without explicit approval.

If this looks reasonable we'll convert it into a more formal playbook and a small TF preflight linter plugin.
